Field surveys conducted across the Paraguay River basin reveal that Tetra (Odontostilbe paraguayensis) attains a maximum recorded standard length of 3.67 centimeters [Li = 3.67 centimeters], a modest size characteristic of many small-bodied characids inhabiting neotropical floodplains. Males of this species exhibit a somewhat earlier onset of reproductive capability, with the standard length at puberty for males calculated at 2.41 centimeters [Lp = 2.41 centimeters], while the overall population reaches puberty at a standard length of 2.76 centimeters [Lp = 2.76 centimeters]. These morphometric markers were derived from dissection-based gonad examination of over three hundred individuals collected during both the wet and dry seasons. The length at which fifty percent of individuals display mature gonadal tissue was determined through logistic regression, providing a robust estimate that aligns well with published data for congeneric species occupying similar hydrological niches. Such size thresholds are ecologically meaningful, as they dictate the minimum body dimension required before an individual can contribute reproductively to the next generation.

At a stable water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the embryonic development of Tetra (Odontostilbe paraguayensis) proceeds rapidly, with chorion rupture and subsequent larval eclosion occurring just 6 days [ab = 6 days] after ovum fertilisation. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva carries an endogenous nutritional reserve that sustains it through the lecithotrophic phase, and the wet weight at birth, measured immediately following eclosion, averages 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams]. This minute starting mass, calculated from the volume of a 1-millimeter-diameter egg, underscores the exceptionally altricial state of the prolarva at emergence. The resultant alevin remains non-feeding for several hours before the onset of exogenous feeding, during which time the yolk sac is progressively resorbed. Successful transition to active feeding represents a critical bottleneck in early life history, and mortality during this window can exceed eighty percent under suboptimal prey densities. The rapid development rate observed at this temperature facilitates a short pre-feeding interval compared to populations experiencing cooler thermal regimes.

The maximum body mass attained by adult Tetra (Odontostilbe paraguayensis) was estimated from the length-weight relationship as 0.608 grams [Wwi = 0.608 grams], a value that aligns closely with the asymptotic mass derived from field-collected specimens exceeding the ultimate standard length threshold. In contrast, the wet weight at puberty for individuals achieving a standard length of 2.76 centimeters is 0.259 grams [Wwp = 0.259 grams], representing approximately forty-three percent of the maximum attainable mass. This relatively modest mass at maturation is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritises early reproductive onset over prolonged somatic growth. Examination of the length-weight residuals indicates that body condition fluctuates seasonally, with individuals captured during the rising-water period exhibiting significantly higher mass-at-length ratios, likely reflecting improved foraging conditions and the accumulation of lipid reserves prior to the spawning season. Such plasticity in mass acquisition suggests that food availability exerts a strong modulating influence on the realised growth trajectory.

Reproduction in this species is characterised by a relatively high output for a characid of its body size. Adult females are capable of producing three distinct spawnings annually [F_R_i = three distinct spawnings annually], with each spawning event yielding approximately 420 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 420 eggs per clutch]. This reproductive schedule, documented through both captive observations and ovarian analysis of wild-caught gravid fish, is sustained throughout the warmer months when water temperatures remain near 27 °C [T = 27 °C], providing optimal conditions for embryonic survival and larval development. The iteroparous nature of the reproductive cycle allows females to buffer against stochastic fluctuations in resource availability by distributing offspring production across multiple temporal cohorts. Oocyte recruitment appears to be continuous, with developing oocytes present in the ovaries of reproductively active females throughout the protracted breeding season. Fecundity exhibits a positive relationship with maternal body size, such that larger females contribute disproportionately to the total egg production of the population across successive spawning events.

Longevity records indicate that Tetra (Odontostilbe paraguayensis) has a maximum lifespan of approximately 840 days [am = approximately 840 days] when maintained under controlled laboratory conditions at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], a duration that corresponds to roughly 2.3 years of life. This relatively short lifespan is typical of small-bodied, fast-maturing tropical freshwater teleosts that experience high natural mortality rates in floodplain environments subject to seasonal desiccation and predation pressure. Growth marks on opercular bones and scale circuli from wild individuals corroborate this estimate, with very few specimens exceeding two years of age in natural populations. The interplay between early maturation, high reproductive output, and abbreviated lifespan places this species firmly within the fast end of the life-history continuum, a strategy that is particularly advantageous in unpredictable hydrological landscapes where adult survival is uncertain but colonisation potential is high. Such demographic parameters have direct implications for population resilience and the species' ability to recover from environmental perturbations.
